takeaway: Consumers can still buy but need a clear reason: lead with value, proof and payment options, and give big-ticket categories more time to convert.

slides.label: Retail sales vs. a year ago
slides.bullet: Spending is running near this year's high, but part of the gain is higher prices: gas station sales are up 28.1% from a year ago. Furniture (+4.9%), building materials (+4.5%) and auto dealers (+2.5%) trail the total.
slides.source: U.S. Census Bureau, Advance Monthly Retail Trade (seasonally adjusted). Released Oct. 15; next release Nov. 17.

chart.title: Retail sales, % change from a year earlier

slides.label: Consumer Confidence Index
slides.bullet: Confidence rose to its highest level since June as gas prices eased, but the Expectations Index (72.6) is still below 80, the Conference Board's recession-signal line.
slides.source: The Conference Board, Consumer Confidence Index. Released Oct. 27; September revised to 84.2.

slides.label: Index of Consumer Sentiment
slides.bullet: Sentiment is at its lowest in five months. Buying conditions for big-ticket goods fell 18% on interest rates and affordability, and consumers expect 4.7% inflation over the next year.
slides.source: University of Michigan, Surveys of Consumers. Final October reading released Oct. 23.

slides.label: Fed districts reporting growth
slides.bullet: Consumer spending was little changed in most districts and led by higher-income households. Price-sensitive shoppers are pushing back on increases, squeezing margins for consumer-facing businesses.
slides.source: Federal Reserve Beige Book, released Oct. 14 (information collected through Oct. 5).
